recipes.title: Velvet Ristretto
recipes.description: A short, syrupy ristretto — high intensity, rounded sweetness and a clean finish.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested coffee, even distribution, level puck and straight tamp matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a small espresso cup, about 45–60 ml.
Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand; distribute evenly, level the puck and tamp straight.
Brew a short ristretto to about 18–22 ml, stopping while the texture is still syrupy and sweet.
Serve immediately while the crema and aroma are fresh.
recipes.proTip: Stop the shot while sweetness is still leading; ristretto is a short cut, not a small normale.
recipes.serve: 45–60 ml warm cup; serve within seconds of the pour.

recipes.title: Doppio Ristretto
recipes.description: A double ristretto in one cup — dense body, layered crema and concentrated sweetness.
recipes.espresso: Espresso standard: 36–44 ml fresh double ristretto.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Keep the cup small, and treat timing as a guide rather than a fixed rule.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a small 60–75 ml cup.
Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand; distribute evenly, level the puck and tamp straight.
Brew a doppio ristretto to about 36–44 ml total, stopping before the flow turns thin or harsh.
Serve immediately while the crema is still intact.
recipes.proTip: If one side runs faster, fix distribution and puck symmetry before changing the grinder.
recipes.serve: 60–75 ml warm cup; serve immediately, not as a large demitasse drink.

recipes.title: House Espresso
recipes.description: A fresh single espresso of about 30–35 ml—balanced crema, clear aroma and a short finish.
recipes.setup: Espresso works best with freshly roasted beans that have rested after roasting; around 10 days to 2 weeks after roast is often a useful starting window, depending on roast and storage.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a small espresso cup, about 50–70 ml.
Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand; distribute evenly, level the puck and tamp straight.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml.
Serve immediately while the crema and aroma are fresh.
recipes.proTip: Taste the shot before adjusting: grind, yield and puck prep matter more than the clock alone.
recipes.serve: 50–70 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Double Shot Doppio
recipes.description: Two fresh espressos in one cup, about 60–70 ml total—rich body, longer finish and more intensity than a single.
recipes.espresso: Espresso standard: 60–70 ml fresh double espresso.

Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand; distribute evenly, level the puck and tamp straight.
Brew a double espresso, about 60–70 ml total.
Serve immediately while crema and aroma are fresh.
recipes.proTip: A doppio that tastes flat in milk was usually flat on its own—fix the shot first.
recipes.serve: 70–90 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Triple Shot Espresso
recipes.description: Three fresh espressos in one cup, about 90–105 ml total—very strong, aromatic and fast to drink.
recipes.espresso: Espresso standard: 60–70 ml fresh double espresso.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a 130–150 ml cup.
Prepare each puck evenly: distribute, level and tamp straight.
Brew three fresh espressos to about 90–105 ml total.
Serve immediately while the aroma is still fresh.
recipes.proTip: Consistency matters more than volume here; the third pull should not run faster than the first.
recipes.serve: 130–150 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Quad Shot Espresso
recipes.description: Four fresh espressos in one cup, about 120–140 ml total—maximum espresso strength for a very intense short drink.
recipes.espresso: Espresso standard: 60–70 ml fresh double espresso.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.

Prepare each puck evenly: distribute, level and tamp straight.
Brew four fresh espressos to about 120–140 ml total.
Serve immediately; do not hold it on the counter.
recipes.proTip: Watch flow and service timing; coffee that waits tastes flat faster than a single.
recipes.serve: 160–180 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Espresso Lungo
recipes.description: A single espresso pulled longer from the machine, about 50–65 ml—more open and drier than espresso, not topped with water.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a 70–90 ml cup.
Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand and prepare an even puck.
Brew one longer machine extraction to about 50–65 ml; do not add hot water afterwards.
Serve immediately while it is still aromatic; it should taste more open and drier than espresso.
recipes.proTip: Espresso lungo is a longer extraction from the machine, not an espresso topped up with water.
recipes.serve: 70–90 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Short Black
recipes.description: A straight single espresso, about 30–35 ml, served black in a small warm cup.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.

Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand; distribute evenly, level the puck and tamp straight.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml.
Serve immediately; a short black is a straight espresso, not a lengthened drink.
recipes.proTip: Treat short black as espresso service: cup heat, freshness and balance matter more than adding volume.
recipes.serve: 50–70 ml warm cup; serve immediately.

recipes.title: Long Crema Americano
recipes.description: Fresh espresso lengthened with hot water in a 180–220 ml cup—aroma opens, bitterness softens and the cup stays bright.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Add 120–150 ml hot filtered water to a warm 180–220 ml cup.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml.
Pour the espresso into the hot water and stir once if needed.
Serve immediately while hot; americano is espresso plus water, not a long machine extraction.
recipes.proTip: Use water you would drink straight—flat or chalky water flattens the cup. For more body, pull a double espresso into the cup and pour hot water into that same cup while the espresso is still extracting (the shot must still be running). Do not wait until the pull finishes and then top up—water after a finished shot is a weaker, different build.
recipes.serve: 200–240 ml preheated cup; hand hot, not lukewarm from the pass.

recipes.title: Long Black
recipes.description: Hot water first, fresh espresso on top—similar volume to americano but with more crema and a sharper aroma.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Add hot filtered water to a warm 160–200 ml cup first.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml, over the water so the crema stays visible.
Do not stir unless needed; keep the aroma and crema on top.
Serve immediately while hot.
recipes.proTip: Long black is about order: water first, espresso last.
recipes.serve: 160–200 ml warm cup; crema visible on top.

recipes.title: Red Eye
recipes.description: Fresh brewed coffee reinforced with one espresso—more caffeine and body without turning into an americano.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Brew fresh filter or batch coffee and pour 160–190 ml into a warm 200–240 ml cup.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml.
Add the espresso to the brewed coffee and stir once if needed.
Serve hot and fresh; this is brewed coffee reinforced with espresso, not an americano.
recipes.proTip: Do not replace brewed coffee with hot water; the brewed base is what makes it a Red Eye.
recipes.serve: 200–240 ml warm cup; serve hot and fresh.

recipes.title: Black Eye
recipes.description: Fresh brewed coffee reinforced with two espressos—stronger and heavier than a Red Eye.
recipes.espresso: Espresso standard: 60–70 ml fresh double espresso.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Brew fresh filter or batch coffee and pour 150–180 ml into a warm 220–260 ml cup.
Brew two fresh espressos, about 30–35 ml each.
Add both espressos to the brewed coffee and stir once if needed.
Serve hot and fresh; this is stronger than a Red Eye and should not be diluted into an oversized cup.
recipes.proTip: A Black Eye should taste like brewed coffee with espresso force, not like a large americano.
recipes.serve: 220–260 ml warm cup; serve hot and fresh.

recipes.title: Gentle Lungo
recipes.description: A longer espresso-style extraction, about 130–180 ml, made with a coarser grind, slightly faster flow and softer body than espresso.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a 180–220 ml cup.
Use a slightly coarser grind than espresso and, where your basket allows, a slightly lighter dose.
Prepare an even puck and extract a longer lungo directly from the machine, about 130–180 ml.
Serve immediately; it should taste softer and less intense than espresso, with a drier bitter edge.
recipes.proTip: Lungo is built by changing extraction, not by diluting espresso after the fact.
recipes.serve: 180–220 ml warm cup; softer, longer and slightly more bitter than espresso.

recipes.title: Caffè Crema
recipes.description: Swiss-style long espresso extraction, about 90–120 ml from the machine, with a golden crema cap and softer intensity than espresso.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a 120–150 ml cup.
Use a coarser espresso-style grind so the coffee can flow longer without tasting harsh.
Extract 90–120 ml directly from the machine into the cup; do not add hot water afterwards.
Serve immediately while the golden crema cap is still fresh.
recipes.proTip: Caffè crema belongs with long espresso-style extraction, not americano-style dilution.
recipes.serve: 120–150 ml warm cup; golden crema on top, no added water.

recipes.title: Americano Misto
recipes.description: Americano lengthened with hot water and softened with a small pour of steamed milk—lighter than a latte, rounder than black americano.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine and steam wand where possible. At home without a steam wand, brew a fresh espresso or strong espresso-style coffee, warm the milk to about 60–65°C until hot but not simmering, then froth with a handheld frother, French press or tightly closed jar for 10–20 seconds. Tap and swirl to break large bubbles; pour while glossy and stop before the foam turns dry. For dairy and plant-based options, test the exact supplier and variant because texture and flavour differ even within the same family.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Add hot filtered water to a warm 200–220 ml cup.
Brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml, and pour it into the hot water.
Heat and lightly texture the milk to about 60–65°C; keep the foam smooth, not thick.
Top the americano with the steamed milk and stir once if needed.
Serve immediately while hot and balanced.
recipes.proTip: Keep the milk small: the goal is to soften the americano, not build a latte.
recipes.serve: 200–220 ml warm cup; serve hot, not reheated.

recipes.title: Guest Lot Espresso
recipes.description: A rotating guest coffee served as espresso to highlight origin, processing and roast character in a small cup.
recipes.setup: Use an espresso machine where possible. Freshly roasted, properly rested beans, even distribution, levelling and straight tamping matter more than following a fixed time blindly.
ingredients: Coffee beans — dose varies by basket; not a universal gram value
recipes.methodTitle: How to make it at home
method: Warm a small espresso cup.
Prepare an even puck and brew one fresh espresso, about 30–35 ml.
Serve immediately with one short note on the coffee origin or flavour character.
Keep the storytelling brief: one useful tasting cue is better than a lecture.
recipes.proTip: Guest espresso is not a new drink build; it is an espresso service that puts the coffee lot and its story in focus.
recipes.serve: 50–70 ml warm demitasse; optionally serve with a small glass of water and one clear tasting cue.

recipes.title: House Drip Coffee
recipes.description: Automatic drip brew—bright acidity, clear sweetness, smooth body; batch consistency for high-volume service.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and batch window to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 17 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the drip-filter grind; rinse/preheat if possible, dose evenly, settle the basket and level the coffee bed.
Start the brewer and confirm the bed wets evenly rather than tunnelling down one side.
Target 4:00–6:00 total brew time; too fast tastes thin, too slow tastes dry and bitter.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Serve fresh and do not keep drip coffee past the house holding window.
recipes.proTip: Automatic drip still needs dial-in; if the machine is fixed, grind and dose are your control points.
recipes.serve: 250–300 ml preheated mug; serve hot, offer refills only while the batch is in window.

recipes.title: Filter Coffee
recipes.description: Paper-filter brew—clean cup, bright acidity and tea-like finish when grind, water and drawdown line up.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 17 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the filter grind; rinse paper, preheat the brewer, dose evenly, settle the grounds and level the coffee bed.
Bloom with enough water to wet all grounds for 30–45 seconds.
Pour clean filtered water in controlled pulses, keeping the bed level and avoiding high dry walls.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Target 2:45–4:00 total drawdown for a 250–320 ml cup; serve immediately while the aroma is clean and sweet.
recipes.proTip: Drawdown is a diagnostic, not a trophy: use it with taste to decide whether to grind finer, coarser or pour calmer.
recipes.serve: 250–300 ml into a warm cup; serve while the aromatics are fresh.

recipes.title: Batch Brew Coffee
recipes.description: Batch filter for volume service—consistent ratio, even extraction, bright filter cup at café scale.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and batch window to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 16 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the batch-filter grind; rinse/preheat where the brewer allows, dose evenly, settle the basket and level the coffee bed.
Start the batch and check that the spray pattern wets the bed evenly during the first minute.
Target 4:00–6:00 total brew time for a standard batch; adjust grind before changing recipe ratio.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Serve within the house holding window; discard coffee that tastes hollow, baked or stale.
recipes.proTip: Batch brew earns trust through repeatability: log dose, yield, grind, brew time and discard time every service.
recipes.serve: 250–300 ml preheated mug; serve hot within your posted batch window.

recipes.title: By-the-Cup Pour-Over
recipes.description: Manual filter brew—clear aromatics, bright acidity and a light body when the pour and grind are controlled.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 22 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the pour-over grind; rinse paper, preheat the brewer, dose evenly, settle the grounds and level the coffee bed.
Bloom for 30–45 seconds so the bed wets evenly and releases gas before the main pours.
Pour in calm pulses or a steady spiral, keeping the bed level and the flow controlled.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Target 2:45–3:45 total drawdown for a 250–320 ml cup; serve immediately and do not hold the brew.
recipes.proTip: A premium pour-over should taste cleaner because it is controlled, not because it is slower for theatre.
recipes.serve: 250–320 ml carafe into a warm 200–260 ml cup; serve fresh.

recipes.title: Chemex
recipes.description: Chemex filter brew—exceptional clarity, floral highs, clean sweet finish; thicker paper, slower drawdown.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 18 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to a medium-coarse Chemex grind; rinse the thick paper thoroughly, preheat the brewer, dose evenly and level the bed.
Bloom for 35–45 seconds, then pour in wide, calm spirals without flooding the filter cone.
Keep the bed level and target 4:00–5:30 total drawdown, depending on batch size.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Swirl the finished brew in the carafe and serve while the clarity and aromatics are still high.
recipes.proTip: Chemex is a clarity brewer; rushed pours or an under-rinsed filter make a premium coffee taste papery and flat.
recipes.serve: 300–320 ml carafe into a preheated 260 ml cup; first pour at the bar.

recipes.title: AeroPress Coffee
recipes.description: Immersion and pressure brew in one—full body, low bitterness, flexible recipe; bright cup with forgiving dial-in.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 16 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the AeroPress grind; rinse/preheat as needed, dose the coffee, settle it evenly and level the bed before brewing.
Add clean filtered water, start the timer, stir or swirl only enough to wet all grounds, then steep for 1:30–2:30 depending on the recipe.
Press steadily for 20–30 seconds without forcing the plunger; stop if the bed compacts harshly.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Serve immediately, or bypass with hot water only if the house recipe is designed for a longer cup.
recipes.proTip: AeroPress is fast immersion: time controls sweetness, pressure controls texture; do not turn it into a forced espresso substitute.
recipes.serve: 250–280 ml into a warm cup; drink while aroma still rises from the surface.

recipes.title: French Press Coffee
recipes.description: Full-immersion press—heavy body, rustic texture, low-acid comfort; oils in the cup, not trapped in paper.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 18 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to a coarse press grind; preheat the French press, dose the coffee, settle it evenly and level the bed before adding water.
Add clean filtered water, saturate all grounds and steep for 4:00.
Break the crust gently, skim heavy foam/fines if desired, then press slowly without forcing sediment through the mesh.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Decant immediately into cups or a server so the coffee does not continue extracting in the pot.
recipes.proTip: French press is not a holding vessel; the brew must leave the grounds when the extraction window is reached.
recipes.serve: 280–300 ml preheated mug; serve hot, not scorching.

recipes.title: Moka Pot Coffee
recipes.description: Stovetop pressure brew—dense, espresso-like intensity without the machine; cocoa notes, small cup, Italian home style.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 17 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to a moka grind; fill the lower chamber with hot water to the valve, dose the basket evenly, level it and do not press the coffee down.
Assemble safely and brew on medium heat; coffee should begin flowing steadily without violent spurting.
Target about 3:00–5:00 from heat-on to finish, depending on pot size and stove; remove from heat before harsh sputtering.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Cool the base briefly under running water if needed to stop extraction, then serve immediately or use as a strong home coffee base.
recipes.proTip: Moka quality depends on stopping before the bitter sputter; the pot is pressure-assisted, not espresso.
recipes.serve: 150–180 ml warm cup; drink while steam still rises.

recipes.title: Flash-Chilled Coffee
recipes.description: Hot filter brew flash-chilled over ice—Japanese-style clarity with cold refreshment; aroma locked, acid bright.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 17 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
Hard ice cubes — 100 ml; enough to chill and serve; use fresh hard ice, not soft or wet ice
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the filter grind; rinse paper, preheat the brewer if needed, dose evenly, settle the grounds and level the coffee bed.
Use a planned hot-water-to-ice split, then brew the stronger hot filter coffee directly over measured hard ice.
Target 2:45–3:45 hot drawdown; swirl once so the intended ice melts and chills the brew fast.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Pour into a 300–350 ml glass with fresh hard ice if needed and serve immediately while the aromatics are bright and the cup is cold.
recipes.proTip: Flash-chilled coffee is the fast service alternative to cold brew: hot extraction, measured ice and immediate chill, not shaken espresso.
recipes.serve: 300–350 ml glass over full ice; Serve cold, kept cold and served immediately.

recipes.title: Iced Filter Coffee
recipes.description: Filter coffee served over ice—bright, clean, refreshing; brew strong or flash-chill so dilution stays in control.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose and water as a starting recipe; adjust grind, water and drawdown to the coffee, brewer and target cup.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 17 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
Hard ice cubes — 120 ml; enough to chill and serve; use fresh hard ice, not soft or wet ice
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to the filter grind; rinse paper, preheat the brewer if needed, dose evenly, settle the grounds and level the coffee bed.
For best clarity, brew stronger hot filter coffee directly over measured hard ice and target 2:45–3:45 total drawdown.
If brewing hot first, chill rapidly and never pour warm coffee over weak service ice.
Use the timer as a dial-in check, not a pass/fail rule: weigh the coffee dose in g and brew water in ml, keep the water quality consistent, then adjust only one variable at a time after tasting.
Serve cold over hard ice while the flavour is bright and clean.
recipes.proTip: Iced filter should be designed around dilution; warm brewed coffee over random ice is not a recipe.
recipes.serve: 300–350 ml glass over full ice; straw optional.

recipes.title: Slow Cold Brew
recipes.description: Traditional 12–18 hour cold steep—low acid, round sweetness and cocoa/nut depth; rapid cold extraction only when validated against the house long-steep batch.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose, water and steep time as a batch recipe; adjust grind, filtration and dilution to the coffee and service strength.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 72 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method
Hard ice cubes — 100 ml; enough to chill and serve; use fresh hard ice, not soft or wet ice
method: Grind freshly roasted beans (ideally 10–14 days after roasting and properly rested) on demand to a coarse cold-brew grind; add coffee and cold filtered water to the brewing recipient, stir until all grounds are fully wet, cover, then steep cold.
Traditional method: steep cold for 12–18 hours under refrigeration or a validated cold-service process, then filter cleanly so no grit reaches the glass.

Rapid-service option: use a validated rapid cold extraction system only—ultrasonic, pressure/vacuum-assisted or controlled recirculation extraction—then fine-filter, chill and taste against the house 12–18 hour batch before service.
Treat the steep time as valid only with the logged coffee dose in g, water ml, coarse grind and water quality; taste the filtered batch before dilution or service.
Dilute to drinking strength with clean cold water and serve over hard ice, or neat if the guest wants a stronger cup.
recipes.proTip: Fast cold brew is a production method, not a shortcut in standards: validate rapid extraction by taste, clarity, strength and filtration before selling it.
recipes.serve: 350–400 ml tall glass over full ice; straw optional.

recipes.title: Nitro Cold Brew
recipes.description: Cold brew infused with nitrogen—cascading crema, creamy mouthfeel, softer bitterness, extra sweetness without milk.
recipes.setup: Treat the dose, water and steep time as a batch recipe; adjust grind, filtration and dilution to the coffee and service strength.
ingredients: Coffee beans — 72 g; freshly roasted and ground on demand for the listed brew method

method: Fill a chilled glass with hard ice.
Brew one fresh espresso, 30–35 ml and pour it over the ice while fresh.
Add cold whole milk and stir once if you want an even colour.
Serve immediately before the ice over-dilutes the coffee.
recipes.proTip: Lukewarm milk coffee is almost always warm milk in the build—fix cold chain before you blame the shot. Brew espresso fresh, then cool it immediately before building over ice; warm espresso over-dilutes the drink and dulls aromatics.
recipes.serve: 300 ml glass; ice and milk measured so the cup still feels like coffee, not water.

recipes.title: Peter's Chilly Choffy
recipes.description: A dense cold chocolate-coffee shake with dark ganache, coffee ice cubes, cold milk and vanilla ice cream.
ingredients: Cold brew or chilled espresso — 30 ml
method: Chill the glass and keep the milk and ice cream cold.
Whisk or blend the liquid dark chocolate ganache with a small splash of cold milk until smooth.
Add the cold brew or chilled espresso and coffee ice cubes, then blend just enough to chill and flavour the base.
Add the ice cream last and blend only until thick and pourable.
Serve immediately while cold; chocolate-heavy cold drinks thicken as they stand.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: 300–350 ml chilled glass with straw; add a small chocolate garnish only when it supports the serve.

recipes.title: Peter's Creamy Dream
recipes.description: A caramel-chocolate dessert coffee with fresh espresso and caramelised pecans: rich, sweet and built as a dessert serve, not a standard latte.
ingredients: Milk or tested plant-based milk — 200 ml
method: Brew one fresh espresso, 30–35 ml.
Add the finely chopped or grated white chocolate to the cup; pour the full fresh espresso over it and stir until glossy. Use a small splash of hot milk only if needed to fully loosen the chocolate.
Add caramel syrup, fine sugar and fine sea salt, then stir again until the base is glossy and even.
Stir until no white chocolate, sugar or caramel sits at the bottom before adding the milk.

While the espresso is still extracting, warm the selected dairy or plant-based milk to 60–65°C. With no steam wand, use a handheld frother, French press or tightly closed jar for 10–20 seconds, then tap and swirl until large bubbles disappear and the surface looks glossy.
While the espresso is still extracting, texture the dairy or plant-based milk into fine, glossy microfoam; small, stable bubbles give a smoother look and creamier mouthfeel than coarse foam.

Pour the steamed or textured milk steadily into the smooth white-chocolate espresso base, integrating it as you pour; finish with only a brief gentle stir if white-chocolate streaks remain at the edge or bottom.
Finish with pecans after the drink is smooth so they stay aromatic and crunchy.
Serve immediately while the drink is warm, glossy and balanced.
recipes.proTip: If it tastes too sweet, reduce the syrup slightly next time. Keep the espresso strong, because the coffee balances the chocolate and milk.
recipes.serve: Warmed clear 280–320 ml glass showing caramel, white-chocolate milk, espresso and foam layers.

recipes.title: Peter's Grand Pom-Pom
recipes.description: Warm apple-pomegranate juice, dark chocolate and Grand Marnier finished with cream, pomegranate and chocolate curls.
ingredients: Lightly whipped cream or plant-based whipping cream — 40 ml
method: Warm the apple-pomegranate juice gently in a small pan; do not boil it.
Whisk the finely chopped or grated dark chocolate with a small splash of the warm juice until smooth and glossy, then add the rest of the juice.
Measure Grand Marnier into the warm chocolate-fruit base and stir once off the heat.
Pour into a warm cup or glass.
Lightly whip the cream and float it on top, then finish with pomegranate seeds and dark chocolate curls.
Serve immediately while the fruit, chocolate and orange liqueur are still aromatic.
recipes.proTip: Fruit acidity sharpens under high heat. Keep the base below boiling and add Grand Marnier late for clean orange aroma.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a warmed 260–300 ml glass with cream, pomegranate and dark chocolate garnish.

recipes.title: Peter's Cuban Kiss
recipes.description: A warm chocolate-coffee cocktail with rum, cream and cacao warmth; served as a composed drink, not a boozy mocha shortcut.
ingredients: Dark chocolate ganache or sauce — 25 g
Whole milk or light cream — 120 ml
method: Warm the serving glass or cup, then empty it.
Measure dark rum carefully into the warm glass.
Add dark chocolate ganache or sauce and stir with a splash of hot coffee until smooth.
Brew one fresh espresso, 30–35 ml, or prepare the listed hot coffee base, then pour it into the measured base.
Lightly whip the cream and float it on top instead of stirring it in.
Serve immediately while the coffee is hot and the alcohol aroma is clean.
recipes.proTip: Keep heat under control after the rum is added. Boiling drives off aroma and makes the drink harsh.
recipes.serve: 180–220 ml preheated heatproof glass or cup; serve hot.

recipes.title: Peter's Pretty in Pink
recipes.description: White chocolate, warm milk and beetroot — a soft pink hot chocolate finished with cream and crisp white chocolate pearls.
ingredients: Milk or tested plant-based milk — 200 ml
White chocolate callets or ground white chocolate — 35 g
Lightly whipped cream or plant-based whipping cream — 40 ml
method: Add white chocolate callets or ground white chocolate to a small pan or pitcher.
Whisk in a small splash of milk or tested plant-based milk until it becomes a smooth paste with no dry powder.
Add the beetroot juice and the remaining milk, then heat gently to about 60–70°C while whisking until smooth and pink.
Pour into a warm cup.
Lightly whip the cream and place it on top, then finish with white chocolate crispearls.
Serve immediately before a skin forms on the surface.
recipes.proTip: Start with a paste. Adding all the milk at once makes dry chocolate harder to dissolve.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a clear warmed 240–260 ml glass with pink cream and white chocolate pearls.

recipes.title: Peter's Float Away
recipes.description: An oat-forward chocolate float with coffee depth, cool mint lift and a creamy finish.
ingredients: Dark chocolate ganache or sauce — 30 g
Cold brew or chilled fresh espresso — 40 ml
Vanilla ice cream or oat-based ice cream — 60 g
method: Chill the glass and keep the oat drink and ice cream cold.
Whisk or blend the dark chocolate ganache with a small splash of oat drink until smooth.
Add the cold brew or chilled espresso and fresh mint, then blend or shake briefly until even.
Add the remaining oat drink gradually and mix until glossy.
Add the ice cream last and blend only until thick and pourable.
Finish with fresh mint and serve immediately while cold.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: 250–300 ml chilled glass with spoon and straw.

recipes.title: Peter's Chai Chocolatte
recipes.description: Dark chocolate melted into chai-infused milk — warm spice, real chocolate and a smooth tea-latte body.
ingredients: Chai-infused milk or tested plant-based milk — 200 ml
method: Add dark chocolate callets to a small pan or pitcher.
Whisk in a small splash of chai-infused milk or tested plant-based milk until it becomes a smooth paste with no dry powder.
Add the remaining chai-infused milk or tested plant-based milk and heat gently to about 60–70°C, whisking until smooth and glossy.
Taste before adding more sweetness; most hot chocolate problems come from poor dissolving, not too little sugar.
Pour into a warm cup and serve immediately before a skin forms on the surface.
recipes.proTip: Start with a paste. Adding all the milk at once makes dry chocolate harder to dissolve.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a warmed 220–240 ml cup or glass, with a very fine chai dusting when it is part of the service recipe.

recipes.title: Peter's Sailing Off
recipes.description: Filter coffee, real dark chocolate and port — a warm after-dinner chocolate coffee finished with cream and cocoa nibs.
ingredients: Lightly whipped cream or plant-based whipping cream — 40 ml
method: Warm the serving glass or cup, then empty it.
Measure port carefully into the warm glass.
Stir the finely chopped or grated dark chocolate with a splash of fresh filter coffee until smooth and glossy, then add roasted cocoa nibs.
Add the remaining fresh filter coffee and stir gently.
Lightly whip the cream and float it on top instead of stirring it in.
Serve immediately while the coffee is hot and the port aroma is clean.
recipes.proTip: Boiled port tastes flat and harsh. Add it late and keep the coffee clean; muddy filter coffee makes the whole drink heavy.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a warmed 220–260 ml cup or glass with cream and cocoa nib finish.

recipes.title: Peter's Bed of Roses
recipes.description: Dark chocolate, warm milk and restrained rose — a floral hot chocolate finished with a soft rose cream cap.
ingredients: Milk or tested plant-based milk — 230 ml
Lightly whipped cream or plant-based whipping cream — 40 ml
method: Add finely chopped or grated dark chocolate, rose syrup and rose water to a small pan or pitcher.
Whisk in a small splash of milk or tested plant-based milk until it becomes a smooth paste with no dry powder.
Add the remaining milk or tested plant-based milk and heat gently to about 60–70°C, whisking until smooth and glossy.
Taste before adding more sweetness; most hot chocolate problems come from poor dissolving, not too little sugar.
Finish with dark chocolate garnish after the drink is smooth.
Lightly whip the cream and place it on top as a soft rose cream cap.
Pour into a warm cup and serve immediately before a skin forms on the surface.
recipes.proTip: Start with a paste. Adding all the milk at once makes dry chocolate harder to dissolve.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a warmed 280–300 ml glass or cup with a soft rose cream cap and dark chocolate finish.

recipes.title: Peter's Orange Is the New Pink
recipes.description: Fluid dark chocolate ganache, sparkling rosé and orange blossom — a cold layered chocolate spritz with floral lift.
ingredients: Rosé champagne or quality sparkling rosé — 150 ml
method: Chill the glass and add the orange blossom ice.
Stir the orange blossom water into the liquid dark chocolate ganache until it loosens slightly and looks glossy.
Spoon the ganache base into the glass so it sits below the sparkling layer.
Pour the sparkling rosé slowly down the side of the glass so the bubbles stay alive.
Finish with edible flowers and serve immediately while the glass is cold and the top still sparkles.
recipes.proTip: Temperature is the drink. Warm ganache kills bubbles; stiff ganache will not integrate elegantly. Keep both glass and sparkling rosé cold.
recipes.serve: Serve cold in a chilled coupe or cocktail glass with visible ganache and sparkling rosé layers.

recipes.title: Peter's Straws & Stripes
recipes.description: Strawberry, dark chocolate ganache and warm milk — a layered hot chocolate finished with strawberry cream.
ingredients: Milk or tested plant-based milk — 200 ml
Lightly whipped cream or plant-based whipping cream — 40 ml
method: Chill the glass and keep the milk or plant-based milk cold.
Whisk or blend the liquid dark chocolate ganache with a small splash of cold milk until smooth.
Add fresh strawberries and fine sugar, then blend or whisk until the fruit is part of the base.
Add the remaining milk gradually and mix until glossy and cold.
Lightly whip the cream and add it as a soft finish.
Serve immediately while the fruit and chocolate still taste fresh.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a clear 280–300 ml glass showing strawberry, chocolate and milk layers with strawberry cream on top.

recipes.stem: I Put a Spelt on You
recipes.title: Peter's I Put a Spelt on You
recipes.description: Dark chocolate, spelt milk and a restrained spirulina note: grain-sweet, chocolate-led and green without tasting marine.
ingredients: Cold spelt milk for slurry — 10 ml
Ground dark chocolate for finish — 2 g
method: Add finely chopped or grated dark chocolate to a small pan or pitcher.
Whisk in a small splash of spelt milk until it becomes a smooth paste with no dry powder.
Add the remaining spelt milk and heat gently to about 60–70°C, whisking until smooth and glossy.
Taste before adding more sweetness; most hot chocolate problems come from poor dissolving, not too little sugar.
Pour into a warm cup and serve immediately before a skin forms on the surface.
recipes.proTip: Start with a paste. Adding all the milk at once makes dry chocolate harder to dissolve.
recipes.serve: Warmed 240–280 ml glass or cup with a light dark-chocolate finish.

recipes.title: Peter's What's Up Brew?
recipes.description: Cold brew coffee, dark chocolate ganache and ginger syrup shaken cold: coffee energy with cocoa body and ginger lift.
method: Chill the glass and fill a shaker with hard ice.
Whisk the liquid dark chocolate ganache with ginger syrup until smooth.
Add filtered cold brew coffee and shake briefly with the ice until cold.
Fine-strain into the chilled glass.
Finish with chocolate crispearls and serve immediately while cold and glossy.
recipes.proTip: Keep the ganache fluid but cold. Stiff ganache streaks; warm ganache flattens the cold brew and makes the finish heavy.
recipes.serve: Serve cold in a chilled 200–240 ml glass or cup, nested in crushed ice when used for service temperature control. Target: clean cold brew, rounded cocoa and bright ginger finish.

recipes.title: Peter's Berry-Me-Up
recipes.description: Dark chocolate ganache, drinking yoghurt and elderberry juice shaken cold: tart berry lift with rounded cocoa depth.
method: Chill the glass and keep the drinking yoghurt cold.
Whisk or blend the liquid dark chocolate ganache with a small amount of drinking yoghurt until smooth.
Add elderberry juice and ground cardamom and blend or whisk until the flavour is even.
Fold or blend in the remaining drinking yoghurt until the drink is glossy and cold.
Finish with cocoa nibs and serve immediately while the texture is creamy and fresh.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: Serve cold in a chilled 220–260 ml glass. Target: berry acidity, chocolate roundness and a clean shaken texture.

recipes.title: Peter's Have No Fear, Beetroot's Here
recipes.description: Warm beetroot juice, dark chocolate and whisky — earthy, smooth and gently spirited.
method: Warm the beetroot juice gently in a small pan; do not boil it.
Whisk the finely chopped or grated dark chocolate with a small splash of warm beetroot juice until smooth and glossy.
Add the rest of the beetroot juice and whisk until the base is glossy.
Measure the whisky into a warm glass or cup.
Pour the hot beetroot-chocolate base over the whisky and stir once.
Serve immediately while the drink is warm and the whisky aroma is clean.
recipes.proTip: Beetroot can turn earthy fast. Dark chocolate must lead; beetroot should bring colour and mineral depth, not vegetable heaviness.
recipes.serve: Serve hot in a warmed 220–240 ml glass or cup; mark clearly when whisky is added.

recipes.title: Peter's Mango Django
recipes.description: Dark chocolate ganache and mango served cold in visible layers, with spice only when it supports the tropical chocolate finish.
ingredients: Large ice ball or hard ice cubes — 120 g
Cardamom, chai spice or piri piri — 0.1–0.2 g
method: Chill the glass and keep the mango juice cold.
Whisk or blend the liquid dark chocolate ganache with a small splash of chilled mango juice until smooth.
Add the remaining mango juice gradually and mix until the drink looks glossy.
Add the cardamom, chai spice or piri piri lightly; it should lift the mango, not dominate it.
Pour over the large ice ball or hard ice cubes.
Serve immediately while cold and layered enough to show the mango-chocolate contrast.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: Serve cold in a clear 280–300 ml glass with visible dark ganache base and mango layer. Guest may stir before drinking.

recipes.title: Peter's Blueberry Thrills
recipes.description: Dark chocolate ganache, buttermilk and blueberries blended cold: tangy dairy, fruit freshness and cocoa depth.
method: Chill the glass and keep all dairy or plant-based components cold.
Add liquid dark chocolate ganache to the blender, shaker or cup first so it can mix into the cold base instead of clumping.
Add blueberries, flaxseed and blueberries for garnish next and blend, shake or whisk long enough that these ingredients become part of the texture.
Add cold buttermilk gradually and blend, shake or whisk until the drink looks even and glossy.
Finish with blueberries for garnish after the base is smooth.
Serve immediately while cold; chocolate-heavy cold drinks thicken as they stand.
recipes.proTip: Cold chocolate drinks need texture control: blend until smooth, then stop before the body turns thin.
recipes.serve: Serve in a chilled 260–280 ml glass, with a flaxseed rim when it is part of the service recipe. Target: smooth, cold, tangy and chocolate-rounded.
